This story offers a gentle reminder that even at the pinnacle of artistic achievement, one's origins can remain a source of strength and identity. Terfel's reflections reveal how tradition, community, and culture can fuel a lifetime of creativity—and why representing his "little nation" on the world stage continues to come first for him, every time.

item.title: Chef transforms cocktail leftovers into dishes and desserts on the São Paulo coast
item.description:
At a cocktail bar in Santos, a coastal city in São Paulo state, Brazil, chef Victoria Diene has developed an inventive approach to reducing waste: transforming cocktail byproducts into desserts and savory dishes. At Urbana Coquetelaria, ingredients that would typically be discarded during drink preparation find new life on the dinner menu, creating unexpected connections between the bar and the kitchen.
One striking example pairs a non-alcoholic cocktail called Panis et Circenses with a dessert named Brasileirinha. After clarifying the drink—a process that separates solids from liquids using milk—Diene discovered the resulting solid material could become the base for a mango cheesecake with yogurt. Even the mango peels aren't wasted: toasted until they develop flavors reminiscent of cocoa nibs, they add crunch to the dessert's crumble topping. Another pairing uses the clarified remnants of a gin-based cocktail as a sauce for pulled pork in a sandwich inspired by acarajé, a traditional Brazilian street food. Diene emphasizes that this approach requires deep ingredient knowledge and proper technique to ensure both flavor and food safety.
This story offers a quiet lesson in resourcefulness and creativity. While Diene acknowledges that adopting such practices requires skilled workers and supportive workplaces—resources not always available in the food service industry—her work demonstrates how observation and experimentation can reveal hidden potential in ingredients destined for the trash. It's a reminder that innovation often begins with simply looking more closely at what we already have.

item.title: International Gibbon Day: Stories of threats and survival
item.description:
International Gibbon Day on October 24th draws attention to a sobering reality: all twenty species of these small apes swinging through Asia's tropical forests face threats from human activity. While gibbons are more closely related to chimpanzees and humans than to monkeys, they're often misidentified—a confusion that feeds into a devastating illegal pet trade. Between January and August 2025 alone, gibbon trafficking seizures reached an all-time high with 336 individuals recorded, revealing the scale of a crisis that tears apart entire family groups.
The capture process is particularly brutal. Hunters shoot mothers from treetops and take babies from their bodies, with only one in ten captured infants surviving to reach buyers. Those who do survive often arrive injured or sick at overwhelmed rehabilitation centers across North Sumatra, where underfunded facilities struggle to provide care. The traffickers factor these losses into their business calculations, continuing despite the staggering mortality rate.
Yet amid these dark realities, there are glimmers of hope. In Java's Gunung Halimun-Salak National Park—home to roughly half the world's remaining Javan gibbons—a women's textile collective is creating forest-inspired fabrics that celebrate local plants and gibbons. Through their work, these women have learned about gibbons' vital role as "forest farmers" who disperse seeds throughout their habitat. This story matters because it reminds us that conservation isn't only about stopping harm; it's also about building appreciation and economic alternatives that give communities reasons to protect the wildlife in their midst.

item.title: Where are the jaguars? GPS helps scientists map corridors across 11 countries in the Americas
item.description:
Scientists have mapped the most comprehensive picture yet of jaguar movement across the Americas, revealing both hope and fragmentation for the continent's largest cat. Using GPS data from 172 jaguars tracked across 11 countries — totaling more than 231,000 location records — researchers identified a vast network of core habitats and travel corridors spanning roughly 6.5 million square kilometers.
The study, led by Brazilian researcher Guilherme Costa Alvarenga, found an impressive connected network linking the Llanos, Amazon, Gran Chaco, Pantanal, Cerrado, Caatinga, and Atlantic Forest regions between Argentina and Brazil. Researchers mapped 307 core areas covering 7.75 million square kilometers — about 55% of the jaguar's current range — with roughly half located in protected areas and Indigenous lands. Yet the connectivity is far from complete. Roads, cities, and agricultural development create barriers that isolate populations, particularly in Mexico, Central America, and Brazil's coastal Atlantic Forest. Human density, livestock presence, and habitat conversion emerged as the strongest negative factors affecting jaguar movement, while ecologically productive areas near water proved most favorable.
This matters because isolation threatens the species' genetic health. When jaguars cannot move between populations, inbreeding increases, reducing adaptability and elevating disease risk — a pattern already observed in Atlantic Forest and Central American populations. The research offers a roadmap for conservation, highlighting where efforts to restore corridors, reduce human-wildlife conflict, and protect existing pathways could make the greatest difference for a species whose survival depends on being able to roam.

item.title: Young country diary: A red squirrel examines a nut, right in front of me | Tom
item.description:
For ten-year-old Tom and his family, October means one thing: the annual ferry ride to Brownsea Island off England's south coast, where red squirrels emerge from their summer hiding places high in the trees. The journey from Poole Harbour begins with the castle coming into view, followed by a welcoming committee of curious chickens and showy peacocks on the lawns before the real adventure begins in the woods behind the little church.
The autumn forest offers its own theatre—crunchy and soggy leaves underfoot, mushrooms pushing through the earth and sprouting from rotting logs. Against this backdrop, the island's red squirrels put on their seasonal show, scurrying at high speed as they gather winter provisions. Tom observes how they pause when they notice human visitors, assessing whether the watchers pose any threat before returning to their work. In one perfect moment, a beam of sunlight catches a squirrel examining a nut on a dead log, creating a golden outline around its body.
What makes this gentle dispatch from a young naturalist worth reading is its reminder of what patient observation can reveal. Tom has learned that red squirrels don't hibernate but instead slow down during winter, staying in their dreys and living off stockpiled food—seeds from pine cones, nuts, bugs, and berries. His appreciation for their intelligence and resilience, the way they multitask between foraging and watching for predators, captures something essential about wildlife watching: it teaches us to notice not just beauty, but the quiet competence of creatures going about the serious business of survival.

item.title: The Muslims finding belonging in southern Spain
item.description:
In the mountains above Alora, in southern Spain, Henrietta Szovati and her husband Ajmal Masroor are creating something both old and new. The couple is transforming a remote farmhouse and its surrounding olive groves into the House of Andalus, a project designed to reconnect people with the region's Islamic heritage and the rhythms of the natural world. The landscape itself whispers echoes of that history—place names derived from Arabic, the shimmer of olive leaves, the ancient fortress crowning the town below.
For Henrietta, a British-Hungarian Muslim, the move represents more than a change of scenery. After more than two decades in Britain, where she often felt her faith was filtered through political debate and suspicion, southern Spain offers something different: a place where neighbors know her first as Henrietta—the woman up the track who buys lemons and honey from Juan Garcia, who helps with the olive harvest. Here, she says, practicing Islam feels easier, less entangled in the charged discourse that shadows Muslim life in much of Europe. Spain's own Islamic past, woven into the language and land, creates a sense of familiarity she hasn't found elsewhere.
The story quietly reminds us that belonging is often found in unexpected places—not just in grand gestures, but in the ordinary exchanges between neighbors, in the work of planting trees, and in landscapes that remember more than one history. It's a portrait of someone seeking not just refuge, but rootedness, in a corner of Europe where the past and present exist side by side beneath an immense blue sky.
